MATES_results_analysis

Kyle Morrison

latest update: 20 June 2024

Set up

knitr set up

Load packages

pacman::p_load(tidyverse,
               here,
               stringr,
               purrr,
               kableExtra)

Load data

# Load data sets
MATES_survey_part <- read_csv(here("data", "survey", "MATES_participant_paper_list.csv"), skip = 0) # 4757 8 

dat <- read_csv(here("data", "survey",  "MATES_survey_results.csv"), skip = 0)  # 188 rows 60 columns 

task_vol <- read_csv(here("data", "task",  "MATES_coauthor_details.csv"), skip = 0) # 30 rows 4 columns

task_pap <- read_csv(here("data", "task", "MATES_task_papers.csv"), skip = 0) # 50 rows 1 column

# MATES_task_results 

dat_task <- read_csv(here("data", "task", "MATES_task_feedback.csv"), skip = 0) # 17 rows 48 column

MATES survey

Extracting Survey Participants

# Create a new column with the email address
MATES_survey_part_modified <- MATES_survey_part %>%
  mutate(Email = str_extract_all(correspondence_address, "\\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\\b")) %>%
  unnest(Email, keep_empty = TRUE)

MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct <- distinct(MATES_survey_part_modified, Email, .keep_all = TRUE) # select records with unique titles (removes exact duplicates)
dim(MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct) # 3969 9
## [1] 3969    9
# Number of rows in the data frame
total_rows <- nrow(MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct)

# Number of rows per chunk
chunk_size <- 400

# Calculate the number of chunks needed
num_chunks <- ceiling(total_rows / chunk_size)

# Loop to create each chunk
for (i in 1:num_chunks) {
  start_row <- ((i - 1) * chunk_size) + 1
  end_row <- min(i * chunk_size, total_rows)
  
  # Subset the data frame
  MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct_subset <- MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct[start_row:end_row, ]
  
  # Create the file name
  file_name <- paste("MATES_survey_participants_", start_row, "_to_", end_row, ".csv", sep = "")
  
  # Write the CSV file to the directory
  write.csv(MATES_survey_part_modified_distinct_subset, here("data", "survey", file_name))
}

Select required columns & rows for the plots

dat <-  select(dat, -c(StartDate, EndDate, Status, IPAddress, Progress, Duration, Finished, RecordedDate, ResponseId, RecipientLastName, RecipientFirstName, RecipientEmail, ExternalReference, LocationLatitude, LocationLongitude, DistributionChannel, UserLanguage))

dat <- dat[-c(1, 2), ]

# Table of the data
 kable(dat, "html") %>%
    kable_styling("bordered", position = "left") %>%
    scroll_box(width = "150%", height = "400px")

Senior career researcher NA Author,Reviewer,Editor NA I have heard of an appraisal tool(s) NA Extremely important Reporting the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for several reasons. First, it allows other researchers to replicate the analysis and to verify the results. Second, it provides information about the capabilities and limitations of the software used, which can be helpful for other researchers when choosing software for their own meta-analyses. Third, it helps to ensure that the meta-analysis was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner. Extremely important Reporting the packages used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for the same reasons as reporting the software used. Additionally, it can be helpful for other researchers to know which packages were used to conduct specific tasks in the meta-analysis, such as data extraction, data analysis, and visualization. Very important Reporting the version numbers of the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because different versions of software may have different features and functionality. By reporting the version numbers of the software used, other researchers can be sure that they are using the same software with the same features and functionality to replicate the meta-analysis. Extremely important Reporting the code used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for several reasons. First, it allows other researchers to replicate the analysis and to verify the results. Second, it provides information about the specific steps that were taken to conduct the meta-analysis, which can be helpful for other researchers when developing their own meta-analysis code. Third, it helps to ensure that the meta-analysis was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner. Extremely important Reporting the primary model (or first model) used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand the specific assumptions that were made about the data and the statistical methods that were used. This information is essential for replicating the meta-analysis and for interpreting the results. Very important Reporting a justification for the primary model (or first model) used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because it helps other researchers to understand why the chosen model was the most appropriate one for the data and the research question. This information can be helpful for other researchers when choosing a model for their own meta-analyses. Extremely important Reporting a weighting scheme for effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how the different studies in the meta-analysis were weighted relative to each other. This information is essential for interpreting the results of the meta-analysis. Very important Reporting whether there is non-independence of effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because non-independence can affect the validity of the results. By reporting whether there is non-independence, other researchers can be aware of this potential problem and can take steps to address it in their own meta-analyses. Extremely important Reporting a measure of heterogeneity between effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how much the effect sizes vary across the studies in the meta-analysis. This information is essential for interpreting the results of the meta-analysis. Very important Reporting the moderator variables included in a meta-regression in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how the effect sizes vary depending on the characteristics of the studies. This information can be helpful for identifying the factors that influence the effect size and for developing theories about the underlying mechanisms. Very important Reporting a sensitivity analysis in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to assess the robustness of the results to different assumptions and decisions. By reporting a sensitivity analysis, other researchers can be confident that the results of the meta-analysis are not simply due to the specific choices that were made in the analysis. Extremely important Reporting the total number of studies included in the meta-analysis is important because it allows readers to assess the comprehensiveness of the review and the size of the evidence base. This information is also essential for assessing the generalizability of the findings. Extremely important NA Very important NA Very important NA Extremely important NA Very important NA

Conflicts of interest: Reporting of conflicts of interest is important for assessing the credibility of the meta-analysis.

Funding sources: Reporting of funding sources is important for assessing the potential for bias in the meta-analysis

This should be a major feature of meta-analyses Very important Together with the effect size, all kinds of meta-data are usually reported in a database or table. A very important part of systematic reviews is the critical appraisal of each datapoint used for analysis. Quality criterial need to be defined and each data point should be subjected to those criteria. Authors need to describe how they deal with data points that were rated as problematic in one or more criteria. Such data points could either be excluded altogether, or sensitivity analyses could be performed to check if problematic data points change the result of the analysis. I think the evaluation of the critical appraisal is an important part of the reporting quality. Not sure what the purpose of this MATES evaluation is. I guess checking the actual statistical analyses is one thing, but I think evaluating the whole process of how the data were retrieved, documented, and ultimately grouped or aggregated and selected for any particular analysis might be even more relevant than the reporting of the analysis itself. Where and how are those steps evaluated? (See also previous comment on critical appraisal) NA

It could only be estimate the mean effect, size, or calculate the homogeneity/heterogeneity between effectsize and identify the moderators. In some cases, yes, very important. (but we should also on how the moderators effects are estimated, meta-regression, meta-forest, …). Very important Yes, But not sufficient. If there is a publication biais. What do we do?? I would propose to better handle publication biais directly in the model(e.g. New method (e.g. robust bayesian meta-analysis;), and not analysing it after and say just yes/no. And I often do not totally trust the authors that say that there is no publication biais using visual analysis of funnel plot,…. Very important For me sensitivity analysis are totally different from publication bias. sensitivity analysis are for testing the hypothesis of the model structure, impact of missing data, type of inference (bayesian/frequentists), …. If the authors do not present sensitivity analysis, I could consider it as a kind of p-hacking, perhaps involving debatable model choices Moderately important I would tend to focus more on the accuracy of the estimated effects (i.e., mean effect, confidence intervals, heterogeneity, etc.). For me, the number of included studies is often a “headline effect”, to get published in ‘big’ journals. + we could extract several effect-sizes for une primary study.. But important to clearly have the list of studies and the database , for transparency, reproducibility, and to update the database Very important Important in the forest plot associated to each effect-size. NA I am not sure to totally understand the question. Do the authors present a forest plot, or other type of plot? Yes, important to better communicate the results. But in some cases, graphical presentations of the results are less important (depending on the aim of tha suty, or on the complexity of the study-). Extremely important yes, for transparency, reproducibility, and to update the database. Science is cumulative. I Think there is a big problem in science now for not to publish the database. NA I am not sure to understand this question. Search strings + scientific Databases used + Kappa test + protocol + conflict of interest + … NA NA

Early career researcher NA Author NA I have used an appraisal tool(s) If PRISMA counts, I have followed that tool before (and still attempt to). Very important Yes I think it’s important to note the software used. But I do think you’ll have to be clearer on the ‘software’ to report. For instance, the ‘yes’ example for this item is the citation of RStudio. It’s fine to cite RStudio (I personally love RStudio) but really, the IDE used is not important, the computational language is. I do not care if the author used RStudio, the basic GUI/IDE that comes with R, Vim, Emacs, or even individual notepad windows + the R console: that is simply a matter of how people use the software. The real software in this example is R, the statistical computation language. I highly recommend changing the example as I’m weary of seeing authors cite RStudio yet neglecting R! (By the way, the confusion is very understandable, tons of people mix these up.) Very important This is important, but perhaps additional detail could be given around the packages pertinent to the analysis. I personally use tons of different R packages but citing all of them would be tedious and cluttered (e.g., citing ‘dplyr’, which is just for manipulating data but not so much the analysis). I do see some authors mix this up on occasion. Suggested revision: “Do the authors report the packages used to conduct the analysis (i.e., the computations, statistical models, and inferences comprising the meta-analysis) within the manuscript or supplementary material?” Slightly important I don’t find this item too severely important, but I can see it (e.g., ‘brms’ is still sort of maturing right now so version number could be helpful). But this item is moot if authors share the workflow/code in the supplementary (ideally with, e.g. for R, a sessionInfo() dump somewhere). Or maybe that’s what this item is suggesting anyways – apologies. Extremely important I’m a big advocate of this. But this item may need to generalise to those who don’t use a computational language (lest we discriminate against spreadsheet warriors). Valid meta-analyses can be done without any scripts at all (not that I would ever do/suggest such a thing). Perhaps the item can emphasise a “reproducible workflow” to capture this nuance. NA It’s not clear to me what is meant by ‘first model’ but maybe I’m missing something. I wonder if it might be beneficial to split this item up: as verbal description and as statistical notation. I find the latter to be best when done properly, and usually authors will cover the former in the process anyways. There’s a lot of flexibility/permutations allowed within the statement “multilevel linear mixed-effects” (by the way I just realised the redundancy in that description). However, I do know that not everyone is well-versed in statistical notation and I wouldn’t want that to be too strict a burden, just a nice-to-have. As always, code to reproduce the analysis should most often clarify the model(s) used. Moderately important Justification is clearly important, I’m just not sure if there should always be a strict statement of it. Also, how much of the model has to be justified, exactly? There’s a lot when you think about it. E.g., one could justify the use of: the normal distribution for the outcome of interest conditional on the mean (why not the Gamma or any other distribution?), the assumption of varying effects (e.g. between-study intercept) coming from a common normal distribution, why a predictor variable is modeled as linear vs. nonlinear vs. semiparametric/smooth, and so on. Further, what if the justification was really weak? E.g., “to account for study-specific effects, we used a meta-analytic model” – well sure! Put another way, what if the model was weakly justified and there’s actually much more that could’ve been done within the model and that would’ve been helpful (i.e. so it’s justified, just not mentioned) but it was simply overlooked? Very important Perhaps include “…weighting scheme for effect size estimates or otherwise account for such weights within the analysis…” My thinking is that it might not always be necessary to weight the effect size (i.e. before the statistical model) when you can incorporate the weight into the model itself (e.g. as a measurement error or as an actual weight). Very important The ‘non-independence’ could be clarified a bit more – statistical dependence arises in all sorts of ways within the meta-analysis context. Also, the example here is weak/bland, suggest getting more illustrative examples. Not at all important I assume heterogeneity by default so I’m just not that interested in testing for this. Put another way, if I’m going to use varying (aka random) effects in my model anyways because they’re more efficient (e.g. Andrew Gelman talks a lot about this), then the test is meaningless. According to some, testing for heterogeneity is important when interpreting ‘overall effects’ from meta-analyses; I can see that. But I’m also never interested in such ‘overall effects’ in many contexts as it’s akin to giving the weather forecast for a continent: effects are always conditional, and particularly for environmental sciences, those conditions arise from different studies. So I wouldn’t want to enforce such a test when it’s unnecessary. Extremely important NA Moderately important I view all research as biased in some way, we can’t help it, so publication bias is sneaking around in virtually any meta-analysis. But I also don’t think it’s that straightforward to suss out and funnel plots/Eggers tests can’t do it all. I’m mixed on this one… Suggest at least relaxing the “test or measure” part as it’s not that easily quantified; in its place, some effort to “discuss or acknowledge” the publication bias risk and its possible effect on the inferences of the meta-analysis (which is most important of all). Moderately important In a way, ‘sensitivity’ is addressed by measures such as cross-validation, it just may not be labelled as such. In any case, ‘sensitivity analysis’ needs to be clarified for what specific part of the meta-analysis (the dataset, the statistical model, other inputs, the literature search itself even) this applies to. Extremely important NA Extremely important NA Extremely important NA Extremely important I’m very glad to see this item. It’s so disappointing how rare meta-analyses in my field actually include data! And it’s not even the authors’ data, it’s someone else’s! And it’s usually paid for by public funds, so it shouldn’t belong to any one individual! I’m hoping this helps things. Very important This is usually pretty helpful. I don’t give it ‘extremely’ important just because there could be some cases where, for brevity’s sake, a data description may not be given but if the dataset is available then that may be forgivable (in my opinion). This isn’t that directly quantifiable, but I believe a statement supporting what context(s) the meta-analysis really pertains to would be good. For example, a meta-analysis might be labelled as “global” (this is very common in my field) which actually means, the allowable sources of literature was global in scope. The actual data collected is very often not global – e.g. studies might be concentrated in N. America, Europe, maybe Oceania, maybe some in Asia, but not at all in Africa. My opinion is that “global” is misleading here. What would be better would be to describe what conditions the meta-analysis really cover. For example, if studying responses across major soil orders of the world, report that “of the 32 world reference soil groups, the dataset compiled here represents 18 soil groups (Table X)”. Relatedly, an assessment of exchangeability in observations is critical in my opinion. This is in context of multilevel models – A. Gelman talks a bit about this, as does Richard McElreath. An example of the discussion of this issue in my general field is this paper by Eagle et al. (doi: 10.2134/agronj2017.04.0215). In other words, the observations being compared shouldn’t be apples v. oranges. Don’t be too dogmatic about meta-analysis. Encouraging better reporting is good but meta-analyses are broader than we often give it credit for. I think there’s a lot of issue with that in the meta-analysis literature. For example, many folks fixate on effect sizes but there’s often more ways to analyse data than just through an effect size (and the effect size might harm the analysis in some cases, or just make it less impactful). Dogma leads to formulaic meta-analyses which stifle scientific creativity and critical thinking and which often fail to really progress the science. Best of luck with this endeavour. If this can be a bit more applicable to the environmental sciences than other tools like PRISMA, then I can see this getting adopted fairly easily, which will be a great benefit to the field of evidence synthesis. PhD student NA Author,Reviewer NA I have used an appraisal tool(s) CEESAT Very important NA Very important NA Moderately important NA Extremely important NA Very important This item is slightly unclear. Is by “reporting the model”, you mean reporting the model structure and characteristics? i.e., the response variables, covariates, and random effects? It is of course important, but less so if the code is provided and readers can directly check the model structure and characteristics. Often times, the models are misspecified in the text, and the only way to properly assess the models is to check how they were coded. Some analyses also do not have a “primary” model, but many primary models, and it can be hard to comprehensively describe each model in the main text. Moderately important I am not sure I fully understand this item. Are you asking for a justification as to why this particular type of model or package was used? Or a justification for why some covariates and random effects were fitted? In the former, it is often subjective (e.g., using bayesian vs. frequentist is not always easy to justify). In the latter, more often than not, people fit covariates to address their main hypotheses, and random effects are here to deal with bias. I think this question would benefit from more details about what type of justification are meant here, and for what part of the model. Extremely important Some authors, and I would agree with this definition, would only consider a study a “meta-analysis” if effect sizes are weighted; so it is indeed important. However, I feel like the phrasing of this item is slightly unclear. More details about what “weighting scheme” refers to would be important for people less familiar with these concepts. Phrasing this as “have authors claimed to weight effect sizes estimates?” would be clearer too. It might also be important to add the code as a potential place in which we can find this information. Extremely important The phrasing could be improved here in my opinion, e.g., “Do the authors report sources of non-independence between effect size estimates…” More details would be helpful here too. For instance, if authors have used random effects to account for study-specific effects, then they have accounted for non-independence although they haven’t specifically mentioned words such as “non-independence”. Extremely important NA Moderately important Although rare, there may be small meta-analyses without moderators, which will make this question irrelevant. Here, inspecting figures and the results section could help know what moderator variables were used, although not specifically mentioned in the methods. Very important NA Very important I am confused why the item refers to “sensitivity analysis IN ADDITION to a publication bias test”. These are often very different tests, and should be considered separately. Extremely important NA Extremely important NA Extremely important I could understand why people would not rate this as “extremely important” because if people report e.g., the mean, confidence intervals, and heterogeneity, then most of the results are already presented. However, visualising the results is extremely important to see how variable patterns are (which is not necessarily well captured by mean and confidence intervals; though much better by prediction intervals), and this variation cannot be ignored when making inferences. Extremely important NA Very important A word is missing after “eligible”, I assume the word “study”? By “description” I assume you mean metadata describing each column of the data? NA I think the questions would greatly benefit from more thorough descriptions and examples. Some of the questions require some prior knowledge of meta-analysis and hence can be prone to errors for people not familiar with certain concepts. Precisely defining each term and giving examples of what is expected would make the tool less susceptible to biases and more standardized across authors. NA

Middle career researcher NA Author NA I have used an appraisal tool(s) PRISMA, PICO, PECO Very important The use of software allows us to be more rigorous in the selection of manuscripts and quality analysis, avoiding errors. Extremely important Meta-analyses must be carried out with some software to be more efficient in the statistical analysis of the chosen measure of association. Very important It allows knowing the extensions and types of quantitative analyzes for a meta-analysis that the authors can apply with the software. If the analysis is limited due to the age of the software, the authors may be asked to perform new analyzes with more updated versions. Extremely important The importance of reporting the code used in conducting a meta-analysis is fundamental to the quality of scientific reporting. It allows transparency and reproducibility of the analysis, review of the analysis performed and quality standards that allow the analysis methods used to be reproducible, consistent and comparable to each other. Extremely important Detailed reporting of the first model used in a meta-analysis is key to the quality of scientific reporting as it impacts a clear understanding of how the analyzes were performed. This is essential so that other researchers, reviewers and readers understand the methodological bases of the study. Also reporting the primary model allows other researchers to reproduce the steps and results of the meta-analysis. By knowing the primary model, other researchers can critically evaluate the suitability of the model for the data and objectives of the study. Extremely important Justifying the primary model in a meta-analysis is essential for the quality of the scientific report. This practice ensures transparency in model selection, facilitates the evaluation of its suitability for the data and study objectives, and allows for critical evaluation by the scientific community. Moreover, it improves the reproducibility and continuity of scientific work. Extremely important Reporting the weighting scheme in a meta-analysis is relevant for the quality of the scientific report. This ensures accurate estimations of the effect size, taking into account the variability and sample size of the studies. It facilitates transparency and reproducibility, allowing other researchers to understand and replicate the analysis. Additionally, it helps to manage heterogeneity among studies and is vital for correctly interpreting the results. Detailed disclosure of the weighting scheme in the manuscript and supplementary material allows for critical evaluation and contributes to methodological improvement in the field, strengthening the credibility and robustness of the study. Extremely important This practice is essential for maintaining the integrity and validity of the results, as non-independence can introduce significant biases. It provides transparency and enhances the reproducibility of the study, allowing other researchers to understand and address the complexities of the analysis. Furthermore, it is crucial for a critical evaluation of the heterogeneity among studies and for ensuring accurate interpretations. The disclosure of this information encourages the use of appropriate statistical methods to handle these dependencies, contributing to the methodological improvement of the field. Ideally, authors should detail in the manuscript and supplementary material how non-independence was addressed, which strengthens the robustness and credibility of the research. Very important This practice assesses consistency among studies, providing information about the agreement or variation of results. An appropriate measure of heterogeneity enhances the interpretation of results and the formulation of conclusions. It allows for the identification of potential confounding factors or moderators and demonstrates a rigorous and transparent methodological approach, essential for scientific credibility. Ideally, authors should report which measure was used and how it influences the interpretation of the meta-analysis results, thus strengthening the robustness and reliability of the study. Extremely important Reporting on moderating variables in a meta-regression in a meta-analysis is crucial for the quality of the scientific report. This provides a detailed understanding of how moderating variables influence the relationships studied, significantly improving the interpretation of the results. It allows for the identification of specific conditions or groups where the effects are more pronounced. Transparency and methodological rigor in presenting these variables are essential for other researchers to assess the robustness of the analysis. Furthermore, the discussion on moderating variables can shed light on unexplored areas and guide future research. Authors should detail in the manuscript or supplementary material the selected moderating variables, their reasons for including them, and their expected impact on the results, thereby enriching the understanding and accumulation of knowledge in the field. Extremely important This activity is key to assessing the validity and reliability of the results, as publication bias can significantly alter conclusions. It provides transparency and demonstrates methodological rigor, allowing readers and other researchers to understand the potential limitations of the study. Addressing this bias increases confidence that the conclusions reflect a fair and unbiased synthesis of the evidence. Additionally, identifying publication bias may indicate the need for further research in potentially biased or incomplete areas. Authors should report the techniques used to assess this bias, such as funnel plots, Egger’s tests, or sensitivity analyses, in the manuscript or supplementary material. This practice not only improves the quality of the report but also strengthens the integrity and robustness of the research. Very important Conducting and reporting a sensitivity analysis in a meta-analysis is essential for the quality of the scientific report. This analysis assesses the robustness of the results against variations in methods, assumptions, or study inclusion criteria, providing a crucial measure of the soundness of the conclusions. It helps identify potential sources of bias or variability, thereby improving the credibility and transparency of the study. Furthermore, the findings from a sensitivity analysis can guide future research by highlighting areas of significant impact on the results. Authors should report this analysis along with tests for publication bias, detailing their methodology and its influence on the overall interpretation of the meta-analysis. This practice not only improves the quality of the report but also strengthens confidence in the validity and robustness of the study’s findings. Extremely important Reporting the total number of studies in a meta-analysis is vital for the quality of the scientific report. This information provides insight into the breadth and representativeness of the evidence reviewed, which is crucial for assessing the reliability of the results. A larger number of studies generally implies greater statistical power and reliability. Transparency in presenting this number reflects a rigorous and methodical approach in the research, essential for the integrity of the study. Additionally, it facilitates reproducibility and verification of the analysis by other researchers. Authors should clearly detail the total number of studies and the selection process in the manuscript and supplementary material, allowing for a thorough and critical evaluation by the scientific community and reinforcing the robustness of the meta-analysis. Extremely important Reporting the total number of effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is essential for the quality of the scientific report. This information provides a clear view of the magnitude and diversity of the data analyzed, crucial for understanding the breadth of the phenomenon studied. A greater number of estimates indicates significant data complexity and variety, which is fundamental for a comprehensive evaluation of the study. The transparency and detail in reporting these estimates demonstrate a commitment to methodological rigor and facilitate a better understanding and assessment of the analysis. Moreover, providing this information is vital for allowing verification and reproduction of the results by other researchers, thereby strengthening the reliability and credibility of the study. Authors should detail the total number of effect sizes and their calculation process in both the manuscript and supplementary material, thus contributing to the robustness of the meta-analysis. Very important Visualizations such as forest plots or funnel diagrams significantly enhance the understanding and communication of complex results, effectively summarizing key patterns and trends. These tools make findings accessible to a broader audience, facilitating interpretation for both specialists and non-specialists alike. They are also useful for revealing trends, correlations, and anomalies in the data. The inclusion of visualizations demonstrates transparency and improves the reader’s experience, allowing for a more direct and profound understanding of the study’s findings. Therefore, it is ideal for authors to include such visualizations in the manuscript and supplementary material. Very important This ensures transparency and allows for the reproducibility of the analysis, fundamental elements for the integrity of scientific research. Providing details about the extracted data, such as sample size and outcome measures, enables readers and other researchers to evaluate the quality and relevance of the included studies. It facilitates detailed scrutiny and constructive criticism, thereby contributing to continuous improvement in the research field. Moreover, the availability of this data is invaluable for future research, providing a solid foundation for new studies. Therefore, it is ideal for authors to detail these data in the manuscript, supplementary material, or an external repository, which enriches the transparency and usefulness of the meta-analysis for the scientific community. Very important to evaluate the con-founders and moderators in our main Meta-analysis effects. Extremely important when studies with significant results are more likely to be published than non-significant findings – has dangerous consequences for meta-analyses. Very important A sensitivity analysis is usually included in a meta-analysis because of uncertainty regarding the effectiveness or safety of an intervention. Sensitivity analyses are purposed to gain insight and certainty about the validity of research findings reported. Very important Useful for defining the research question, data collection, data preparation, data analysis, and reporting and meta-analysis. Very important Effect size reporting is crucial for interpretation of applied research results and for conducting meta-analysis. Very important Visualization helps us see the story the data is telling, enabling highly effective reporting practices. Very important Extracting data from studies is the norm in meta-analyses, enabling researchers to generate effect sizes when raw data are otherwise not available. Very important Evaluating the quality of reporting enables interpretation of the current quality of evidence and thus the current state and clinical relevancy. The calculations are spoton and the images are sharp enough for use in publication. The ideal output should be readily digestible by end-users, often clinicians and policymakers, to inform evidence based decision making. NA

Senior career researcher NA Reviewer,Other Reader I have used an appraisal tool(s),No experience not myself Very important NA Very important The utmost important thing happens before MATES comes into play: professional data stratification. This is where ALL meta-analysis in ecology - plant sciences I have seen failed completely. The reason: it is done by non-biology experts, people in maths or stats. Very important standard procedure Moderately important once the software and its version is reported, this seems like less important Extremely important If what you call the ‘first model’ means the basic structure of the analysis, this is possibly the most important step. Qualified data stratification and data sorting by co-variable is the alpha and omega of meta-analysis. The rest is maths Extremely important Most often, the justification of how (and why) data were structured in the way this was done is insufficient. Extremely important If weighing is supposed to indicate the weight of certain frame conditions he data are nested in, this is super important. To give you an example: An analysis for the influence of CO2 on plant growth is completely worthless unless the concurrent nutrition of plants is accounted for in a trustworthy, educated manner. Extremely important There is no such thing as non-independence. That is the central problem of meta-analysis. There is always a confounding influence. We see a flood of meta-analysis (recently mostly from researchers in China), that irons the data flat. Whatever response meta-analysis aims at distilling depends on the quality of the handling of confounding variables. This is not normally something that statistics experts can do. In the end we often see meta-analysis the outcome of which reflects the frequency distribution of methods. For instance, if 95% of the data come from potted plants and 5% from trees in nature, the outcome will be dominated by what potted plants do, no matter how sophisticated the meta-analysis is. Moderately important I cannot answer this. I do not understand the question Extremely important If, what you call ‘moderator variable’ is what I would call confounding variable or interactive variable, that this is the most important of all points. See my earlier comments. Your phrasing reads a bit cryptic to me. Extremely important Again, if this refers to biased data handling (e.g. not stratifying data by things like age of people, or nutrition of plants, or experimental conditions such as indoor vs outdoor etc.) this is key. Extremely important sure you want to see the power of the analysis, for instance how sensitive the analysis is with regard to the inclusion or exclusion of certain criteria by which the data were stratified (sorted) Extremely important Trivial, of course you need to describe your sample and what its structure is Extremely important there should be no such analysis without descriptive stats upfront Moderately important nice to have, but if it hides or masks things because of two dimensional description of what is multidimensional they can also disguise the reality Extremely important you mean descriptive stats upfront? The raw tables with what had been entered into the analysis must be reported in supplementary archives. That archive should already structured in a way how the data were used in the analysis. Extremely important I think this refers to the before mentioned archive. The listing must show the criteria (codes) by which the data were stratified in the analysis The most important thing happens before meta-analysis. I saw only biased meta-analysis because this data handling was left to software and stats people. The sorting of data and the specification of co-variables and interactive terms must be decided by the best experts of the subject. Possible by a consortium of experts. The technical part that follows is of secondary importance. I have not worked with MATES, but I have seen many meta-analysis and actually published two- or three-times on their miserable handling in prominent journals. In all cases the analysis led to highly biased results, because the data were not properly stratified. This is the hard job. Because you need to read and UNDERSTAND the papers in order to rank the data BEFORE entering meta-analysis. NA

Survey Question 1

What is your current stage of career?

# Separate rows and count total 
total_career_stage_count <- dat %>% 
  separate_rows(Q1, sep = ",\\s*") %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Q1)) %>%
  count(Q1) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n))

# Calculate count as a percentage
total_career_stage_percentage <-  total_career_stage_count %>% 
  mutate(proportion = n/sum(total_career_stage_count$n),
         percentage = proportion*100)

# Theme for all MATES plots 
MATES_theme <-  function(){ 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray", linetype = "dashed"),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 1.2),
    axis.line.y = element_line(linewidth = 1.2),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, size = 25, color = "#666666"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 20, color = "#666666"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 20, face = "italic")
  )
  }

# Plot for survey question 1 
fig_Q1 <-  total_career_stage_count %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y =reorder(Q1, n)), hjust = 0.5) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, x = n/2 ,y = reorder(Q1,n)), hjust = 0.5, size = 8, color = "white") +
  geom_text(data = total_career_stage_percentage, aes(label = paste0("(", round(percentage, 1), "%)"), x = n), 
            hjust = -0.1, size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_identity(guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0), limits = c(0, max(total_career_stage_count$n*1.3))) +
  MATES_theme() +
  labs(caption = "Survey Question 1\nThe value in each bar is the total number of participants")

fig_Q1

Question 5

Comments on MATES item 1 (e.g., potential improvements or a justification of response)

# Filter dataframe for question 5
df_Q5 <- dat %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Q5)) %>% 
  select(c(Q4,Q5))

# Table for question 5
 kable(df_Q5, "html") %>%
    kable_styling("bordered", position = "left") %>%
    scroll_box(width = "150%", height = "400px")
Q4 Q5
Extremely important The software used for analysis help reviewers and readers understand the nuances in the methodology used and provide transparency for repeatability.
Extremely important It should be more and more convenient and accessible for authors to use.
Moderately important Analysis methods is more important than software
Extremely important So that it can be replicated. I like R because the code and data can be published. RevMan which a lot of people use has its own format.
Very important Different softwares can have differnet biases, so it has to be reported
Extremely important Reporting the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for several reasons. First, it allows other researchers to replicate the analysis and to verify the results. Second, it provides information about the capabilities and limitations of the software used, which can be helpful for other researchers when choosing software for their own meta-analyses. Third, it helps to ensure that the meta-analysis was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner.
Extremely important This practice enhances transparency and reproducibility in research, allowing readers to understand and potentially replicate the analysis. Providing information about the software used is also crucial for the scientific community to assess the validity of the findings and build upon the research in the future.
Very important State the tools used clearly in the methodology
Very important Each software are based on specific algorithm, e.g. for the tau2 estimators, ….
Extremely important It is important to assist future researchers who are not as experience, but it also allows greater repeatability. i.e., when two different groups argue about responses using two different software is something I have encountered a a reviewer
Very important Systematic review data is complex and has multi-dimensional relationships and therefore the manner in which the data is collated and stored needs to be robust (e.g. in a relational database)
Very important Perhaps be more specific or provide examples of when software would be used (literature screening, analysis etc)
Moderately important No comments.
Very important Since some analyzes may not be performed by all statistical software, it is necessary to mention this point.
Extremely important The used software can affect the quality of the results and respective conclusions.
Extremely important I am still learning
Very important including version
Extremely important no comment
Very important One could generally think of having a more differentiated assessment: Full reporting (including versions), partial reporting and no reporting, to reduce the number of questions. Will make this comment only here but may apply to several questions.
Moderately important This matters less (or doesn’t) if the methods are well and fully described
Extremely important It might be worth splitting the statistical analysis from software used for screening and summarising the inclusion of articles.
Extremely important The type of software is important to work towards a standardization of meta-analysis methods
Moderately important The software alone is not very important. It is more relevant to report (i) the statistical methods/models, and (ii) the code.
Extremely important Perhaps an intermediate response could involve the software for analysis being indicated but other software not. I understand that the questions mainly target the statistical analysis itself. But if the appraisal questions were meant to be broader, software for paper management and screening and for extracting data (plot digitizer…) would also need to be indicated, and failure to do so would involve an intermediate level of response.
Very important processing mode and error level
Very important Yes I think it’s important to note the software used. But I do think you’ll have to be clearer on the ‘software’ to report. For instance, the ‘yes’ example for this item is the citation of RStudio. It’s fine to cite RStudio (I personally love RStudio) but really, the IDE used is not important, the computational language is. I do not care if the author used RStudio, the basic GUI/IDE that comes with R, Vim, Emacs, or even individual notepad windows + the R console: that is simply a matter of how people use the software. The real software in this example is R, the statistical computation language. I highly recommend changing the example as I’m weary of seeing authors cite RStudio yet neglecting R! (By the way, the confusion is very understandable, tons of people mix these up.)
Extremely important This is probably provided later on, but I think authors should also provide their meta-analysis code and data as well.
Extremely important This is an important piece of information that the reviewer should know when assessing the quality of the reported information.
Very important I it important report software to assess the quality of results
Very important Overall approach and full disclosure is necessary. However, quality of analysis should go beyond software usage.
Very important The use of software allows us to be more rigorous in the selection of manuscripts and quality analysis, avoiding errors.
Very important Each tool can be based on certain points, for example, focusing on the keywords existing within the text but it can be used by the author as an example not the main topic of the paper
Moderately important Several softwares are available, better than software, the exact model implemented is very relevant (e.g. random versus fixed model)
Very important Good question.
Extremely important None
Extremely important Synergizing MATES with real time data from different locality
Extremely important The software and packages need to be reported to allow for the MA to be repeated, and for appraisal of potential bias
Extremely important Beside the obvious intent of providing enough info for repeatability, you also acknowledge the work of the people allowing you to do your work,which is fair and ethical.
Extremely important Quality and replication of data
Extremely important As part of the methodology, authors should report the software used to conduct the meta-analysis. This is for transparency, and also to train readers and new researchers in the field.
Very important I think this is very important because different software may yield different results. For example, using Google Scholar vs. Web of Science will likely show different publications. Differences in results may also be obtained if different versions of software packages are used etc.
Very important configuration/options in some software are also important, although those may be covered in other parts of the methodology
Moderately important According to my experience, software is not important for doing meta-analysis, and the results from different softwares are always similar
Very important To ensure accurate comparison, reproduction, and discussion of results, it is crucial to provide detailed information about the software used for analysis. Even slight differences in software versions must be reported.
Extremely important I think it is very important that all steps in conducting the meta-analyses are reported so that the process is as transparent as possible. Beyond reporting the software used, I think it is important to share codes to improve repeatability of analyses and also facilitate learning best practices.
Extremely important It’s extremely important for transparency and reproducibility; and for future updates and revisions.
Moderately important With no knowledge about what such a software does, this question is difficult for me to answer.
Extremely important As in all research, reproducability is important. Therefore, the software used should clearly be stated.

Q6 Q7
Very important The packages used for analysis help reviewers and readers understand the nuances in the methodology used and provide transparency for repeatability.
Extremely important Beside reporting the package used for meta-analysis, some essential methods in the package should be described to facilitate readers’ understanding and appraising the results.
Extremely important Different packages have different methods
Extremely important Same as before
Extremely important Different packages can give different results, so this increases repeatability
Very important Acesso gratuito e cursos
Extremely important Reporting the packages used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for the same reasons as reporting the software used. Additionally, it can be helpful for other researchers to know which packages were used to conduct specific tasks in the meta-analysis, such as data extraction, data analysis, and visualization.
Very important For software that works with packages like R, the reporting of packages is as important as reporting the software itself, because without this information, the reader does not know what was done.
Extremely important It is crucial for transparency and reproducibility in research to provide information about the software used. This allows readers to understand and replicate the analysis, which is important for the scientific community to assess the validity of the findings and build upon the research in the future.
Very important The results could be replicated
Very important Same remark as before. Need also to provide clearly the equation in the main text, (and/or the script in supp mat)
Extremely important Same as comments on item 1
Very important Some analysis should be done with a specific R package.
Very important Perhaps this does not apply to all types of meta-analysis software, but I guess this can be selected as N/A.
Very important Would this apply to all software that would be used, or only a subset?
Extremely important Important for replication of results
Extremely important Still learning MATES
Slightly important To my experience package is imprtant when using R. There might be other metanalysis tools (Sigma Stat, SPSS, Excel)
NA I am not sure i understand the framing “report the packages”. Software packages?
Moderately important I’d rather have the model/methods well described but if not, the package at least gives you a starting point for what was likely done (is assume defaults likely used)
Very important It is vital to reproduce the analysis.
Extremely important The report of software packages is important to work towards a standardization of meta-analysis methods
Very important As said above, it is important to report the code + the statistical methods/models. The sofware and package are useful elements but are not sufficient alone.
Very important so others can see how useful it is and use or not use it.
Very important Need some explanation abuot what packages are.
Extremely important I use R and understand the importance of citing packages. But do all softwares actually have “packages”?
Moderately important I feel that there is overlap between item 1 and 2 and 3, or at least some overlap. I think that this could be simplified into 1 item for which at least some component of these three is mentioned
Moderately important generally the author has the data available to verify what has been reported
Very important Not necessarily crucial if clear within documented code, but ideal.
Very important This is important, but perhaps additional detail could be given around the packages pertinent to the analysis. I personally use tons of different R packages but citing all of them would be tedious and cluttered (e.g., citing ‘dplyr’, which is just for manipulating data but not so much the analysis). I do see some authors mix this up on occasion. Suggested revision: “Do the authors report the packages used to conduct the analysis (i.e., the computations, statistical models, and inferences comprising the meta-analysis) within the manuscript or supplementary material?”
Extremely important May require some language specification as some people use “package” and “software” interchangeably.
Extremely important When reporting the software, it is important to report both the package and the version numbers to ensure latest and appropriate tools have been used in the analysis.
Moderately important Software packages change, but usually not significantly. Relevance of meta-analysis should go beyond versions/packages of software. It’s not a problem if mentioned, but I won’t shot down a contribution because it does not mention software package.
Extremely important Meta-analyses must be carried out with some software to be more efficient in the statistical analysis of the chosen measure of association.
Moderately important The difference between this and the previous question regarding software could be clearer
Extremely important Not only the packages, but also their version.
Moderately important packages Can be changed very fast over time, and it has no meaning to know about not existing package!
Very important Specify the version of the package
Moderately important As before, several softwares are available, generally with one official package for MA.
Very important Important, but keep in mind that “packages” is language most relevant when using R/Python as the analysis platform.
Very important It is important
Extremely important Important for repeatability and appraisal of potential biases
Very important it is important to report the quality or at least have a critical assessment of the quality
Very important Your paper must provide enough information that your work could be repeated. Editors and referees will certainly read your text with an eye for repeatability.
Extremely important Reproducibility
Extremely important As part of the methodology, authors should report the packages used to conduct the analysis. This is for transparency, and also to train readers and new researchers in the field.
Very important It is important if you use software like R. In CMA, it seems not relevant.
Very important Please refer to my comment on the last question!
Very important The utmost important thing happens before MATES comes into play: professional data stratification. This is where ALL meta-analysis in ecology - plant sciences I have seen failed completely. The reason: it is done by non-biology experts, people in maths or stats.
Slightly important Still, this would be useful for other authors to replicate the review, but for meta-analysis itself is not important
Very important If the package has slight differences that can result in distinct outcomes, it will be the same as the previous question. Then is it important report the details.
Very important Reporting needs to be clear and precise, and main packages (and versions used) should be reported. Since the number of packages can quickly add up, additional packages could be listed in the scripts.
Extremely important It’s extremely important for others to understand the methodology, and support the study’s validity.
Moderately important Same remark as before applies here.

Q8 Q9
Moderately important Package versions can be important if substantial changes are made to functions because changes may alter the reproducibility and transparency of analysis. Tight word counts on journals can make this level of detail challenging but I would love to see reporting at this level of detail as standard practice for all papers (not just meta-analyses).
Extremely important Noval versions are generally more preferred.
Extremely important It all goes together, if you say what you are using give the version number. It is probably more important with R than RevMan because R is more dynamic - especially metafor which they do a great job of updating.
Extremely important Different versions can give slightly different results
Very important Reporting the version numbers of the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because different versions of software may have different features and functionality. By reporting the version numbers of the software used, other researchers can be sure that they are using the same software with the same features and functionality to replicate the meta-analysis.
Moderately important version numbers of software packages are part of the reporting in scientific publications. However, the way packages work are often not changing among versions, so maybe moderately important after all.
Very important Understand the up-to-date info
Moderately important I have never really though about this.
Very important Very important, but perhaps I would not expect too much difference between (say) different versions of R
Slightly important Software version numbers change regularly but this shouldn’t significantly alter the quality of the review
Very important To make it clear to different audiences (understanding)
Slightly important Only truly important if major changes to default method made and if actual methods underlying analysis made by program are poorly described.
Very important As before, vital for reproducibility.
Moderately important The version is important for understading the updates of the software at the time of analysis.
Very important See my comment above
Extremely important In some sense I don’t necessarily think something like this is liable to make much difference to the outcomes of the analysis, but it seems so easy to report this information that I can’t see why it would ever be omitted.
Slightly important see my comment on item 2
Moderately important changes in reporting mode, error level, type of functions
Very important Depends on the package or software used, in case there are major updates between versions I would say yes.
Very important Not unresolvable if not, but clearly ideal
Slightly important I don’t find this item too severely important, but I can see it (e.g., ‘brms’ is still sort of maturing right now so version number could be helpful). But this item is moot if authors share the workflow/code in the supplementary (ideally with, e.g. for R, a sessionInfo() dump somewhere). Or maybe that’s what this item is suggesting anyways – apologies.
Moderately important Version number isn’t terribly important if the authors also provide code and data.
Extremely important When reporting the software, it is important to report both the package and the version numbers to ensure latest and appropriate tools have been used in the analysis.
Slightly important see my earlier comment
Very important It allows knowing the extensions and types of quantitative analyzes for a meta-analysis that the authors can apply with the software. If the analysis is limited due to the age of the software, the authors may be asked to perform new analyzes with more updated versions.
Very important Does this need to be a separate question, could the first not be ‘report software and version number’?
Extremely important Nevermind my previous comment
Not at all important The version improved over time mostly to fix errors and add features. Not related to the main functions.
Moderately important This is relevant due to changes across years (e.g. metan before Stata 16 and meta set routine from Stata 16).
Very important This is only really important if there have been changes that impact the results/ introduce bias, so probably safer to include than not
Slightly important the version sometimes refers to specific features which may or may not be relevant. Actually it is not very important for the quality of the analysis as such, but as long as it is stated, it is sufficient. There does not need to be a specific explanation of the version.
Very important Full development In addition to “research ethics”, the presentation of statistical tools and data background is underpinned by a strong focus on systematizing research in order to share current knowledge as well as providing new challenges for pushing forward fresh knowledge.
Extremely important Data quality
Slightly important As part of the methodology, authors should report the software version used to conduct the meta-analysis. But lack of reporting the version, as long as the software is reported should not penalize the quality of the reporting.
Moderately important I think that reporting version numbers of specific packages may be more important. I am not sure how much difference there is between, say, R version 2.1 and R version 2.2, whereas statistical software packages may include calculation improvements etc. But I could be wrong.
Very important standard procedure
Not at all important No

Very important See my previous answer ;)
Moderately important Need the version number for technical support and troubleshooting, if necessary.

Question 10

What is the importance of reporting the code used to conduct the meta-analysis to the quality of reporting?

Referring to MATES item 4:

Do the authors report the relevant code to conduct the analysis within the manuscript, supplementary material or an attached repository?

This information can be helpful for other researchers when choosing a model for their own meta-analyses.
Slightly important I guess the most trivial justification would be that the selected type of model best fits the data. Not sure if such justification needs to be mentioned in the manuscript.
Very important Good to provide rationale of the selection
Very important yes, for me authors should justify why the do not used random effect model, and proper weighting,… (if it is the case).

NA same comment as previous
Very important The challenge here is what qualifies as “justification”? Is it a citation of another paper or book? Or something more substantive?

Moderately important Same comment as the question before
Moderately important Model may be equal to “hypothesis”?
Very important ’-Some papers may not have a primary model but go straight to meta-regression. From my point of view, this would be the criterion to select NA in this question (and it would be a matter for procedural quality, rather than reporting quality). -The criterion specified for “No” is rather long and confusing.
Extremely important Definitely needed as this will give some clues about the extent authors understand the model and its assumptions.
Not at all important Similar to Q12, I don’t understand this question/what primary model means, so I assume it is not important
Moderately important Justification is clearly important, I’m just not sure if there should always be a strict statement of it. Also, how much of the model has to be justified, exactly? There’s a lot when you think about it. E.g., one could justify the use of: the normal distribution for the outcome of interest conditional on the mean (why not the Gamma or any other distribution?), the assumption of varying effects (e.g. between-study intercept) coming from a common normal distribution, why a predictor variable is modeled as linear vs. nonlinear vs. semiparametric/smooth, and so on. Further, what if the justification was really weak? E.g., “to account for study-specific effects, we used a meta-analytic model” – well sure! Put another way, what if the model was weakly justified and there’s actually much more that could’ve been done within the model and that would’ve been helpful (i.e. so it’s justified, just not mentioned) but it was simply overlooked?
Moderately important I am not sure I fully understand this item. Are you asking for a justification as to why this particular type of model or package was used? Or a justification for why some covariates and random effects were fitted? In the former, it is often subjective (e.g., using bayesian vs. frequentist is not always easy to justify). In the latter, more often than not, people fit covariates to address their main hypotheses, and random effects are here to deal with bias. I think this question would benefit from more details about what type of justification are meant here, and for what part of the model.
Very important Could perhaps use some specificity. E.g., why did the authors use fixed/random effects/REML, etc). How did they harmonise across studies, e.g., where one paper used a continuous exposure measure while others used categorical, or one paper used Odds Ratios and another used Relative Risk.
Extremely important Justifying the primary model in a meta-analysis is essential for the quality of the scientific report. This practice ensures transparency in model selection, facilitates the evaluation of its suitability for the data and study objectives, and allows for critical evaluation by the scientific community. Moreover, it improves the reproducibility and continuity of scientific work.
Extremely important Just needs a line or two.
Very important Relevant to provide information of any difference due to model used.
Moderately important See response to previous question
Very important

Also useful for other researchers to gain an understanding re the models and why they are used
Extremely important to provide clear and reliable conclusions, to convey vast amounts of information
Extremely important Readers should understand the reasoning behind including the variables introduced in the models.
Moderately important This might not be crucial for the quality of the study itself because if the type of model was already specified, reproducing the analysis should yield the same results. I think this would be rather important from an informative standpoint and to make the paper more well rounded.
Extremely important Most often, the justification of how (and why) data were structured in the way this was done is insufficient.
Very important If the first model was discarded, it is crucial to know the first approach that the authors used, in order to evaluate the improvements and changes on the final model.
Extremely important I think this answer reflects actually how I understood the previous question
Very important This is for documentation for future reference and for communication of specific choices.

Extremely important Some authors, and I would agree with this definition, would only consider a study a “meta-analysis” if effect sizes are weighted; so it is indeed important. It facilitates transparency and reproducibility, allowing other researchers to understand and replicate the analysis. Additionally, it helps to manage heterogeneity among studies and is vital for correctly interpreting the results. Detailed disclosure of the weighting scheme in the manuscript and supplementary material allows for critical evaluation and contributes to methodological improvement in the field, strengthening the credibility and robustness of the study.

Moderately important it is not relevant to all meta analyses.
Extremely important If this is not reported and one were to repeat the analysis, the results would be different.
Extremely important If weighing is supposed to indicate the weight of certain frame conditions he data are nested in, this is super important. To give you an example: An analysis for the influence of CO2 on plant growth is completely worthless unless the concurrent nutrition of plants is accounted for in a trustworthy, educated manner.
Moderately important This criteria seems more study-specific than the previous metrics
Very important In addition to reporting the weighting, the authors must declare the criteria with which they established the weights of each response to make them comparable between the different studies analyzed.
Extremely important For understanding the sources of heterogeneity and for future reference.

Very important Yes this is important, although just ‘considering’ non-independence isn’t enough. Saying there is non-independence but not explaining what you do about it (if anything) would be problematic and the same as not reporting it.
Very important Most of the paper ignored this information that should be reported.
Extremely important A lot of people won’t understand the importance of this, but it is pretty important because obviously the SE will be wrong if they don’t account for it. Being in the final tool might make people more aware of the issue as well.
Extremely important That is usually need mixed models, so definitly
Extremely important Unfortunately non-independence is seldom properly treated in meta-analyses.
Very important Reporting whether there is non-independence of effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because non-independence can affect the validity of the results. By reporting whether there is non-independence, other researchers can be aware of this potential problem and can take steps to address it in their own meta-analyses.
Very important Question not so clear - I think examples of what types of independence should be considered here would be helpful. There is often some level of dependence in datasets used for meta-analyses and a discussion of that should be done by the authors. Unclear to what extend such discussion should be detailed.
Very important Again, understand more about the limitations and assumptions of the study
Very important Ofen a blind spot in ecological/agronomic meta-analysis. NOt very understood by researcher, I think (or at leat by the students during the training on meta-analysis I give).
Very important Many meta-analyses in my field do not do this, and I think this is important
Extremely important Maybe could also include if the authors have attempted to control for non-independence?
Extremely important Failure to account for non-independence can artificially reduce the amount of variability around effect size estimates and therefore increase the likelihood of false positives.
Very important Need to be very acurate
NA Unsure what is meant by non-independence of effect size estimates
Extremely important I think the question should be reworded to refer to whether they tested for a specific form of non-independence, or if they addressed it in their model. I don’t think the authors can actual report if there was non-independence – in most cases, there certainly is – it’s a matter of detecting it and appropriately addressing it.
Moderately important I am not sure about the importance of this matter…
Extremely important again, the questions isnt well-worded. Of course, if there is non-independence, it should be reported and taken into account.
NA That sounds like a great thing, but not something I have done or know how to do, so I can’t comment. The field has developed since my last meta-analysis (though I have done a systematic review recently)
Very important The ‘non-independence’ could be clarified a bit more – statistical dependence arises in all sorts of ways within the meta-analysis context. Also, the example here is weak/bland, suggest getting more illustrative examples.
Extremely important The phrasing could be improved here in my opinion, e.g., “Do the authors report sources of non-independence between effect size estimates…” More details would be helpful here too. For instance, if authors have used random effects to account for study-specific effects, then they have accounted for non-independence although they haven’t specifically mentioned words such as “non-independence”.
Moderately important Seems important but I’m not too clued up on this aspect. Does this refer to results from the same study/paper? Normally, I would choose only one result if there is dependence between them.
Extremely important This practice is essential for maintaining the integrity and validity of the results, as non-independence can introduce significant biases. It provides transparency and enhances the reproducibility of the study, allowing other researchers to understand and address the complexities of the analysis. Furthermore, it is crucial for a critical evaluation of the heterogeneity among studies and for ensuring accurate interpretations. The disclosure of this information encourages the use of appropriate statistical methods to handle these dependencies, contributing to the methodological improvement of the field. Ideally, authors should detail in the manuscript and supplementary material how non-independence was addressed, which strengthens the robustness and credibility of the research.
Extremely important Important but hardly ever done. They type of non-independence is also important (clustered/correlated due to repeated measures etc.)
Slightly important Not very relevant as the difference may be driven by a p values cutoff (e.g. p<0.05, an approach to dismiss, the use of fixed statistical cutoff.
NA Would effect sizes be non-independent in a meta-regression for which you had multiple data points per paper? If so, a meta-regression may have ways to account for “non-independence” in their modeling framework (e.g., random effects?) without calling out non-independence.
Extremely important By reporting non-independence and describing how it was dealt with, it helps other authors recognizing non-independence within their own data and provides analytical tools that are sound and reproducible
Very important Again, important for assessing potential bias
Extremely important this is the basis for statistical analysis.
NA Non independence can affect two major interrelated components of a meta-analysis: (i) the calculation of effect size statistics and (ii) the estimation of overall meta-analytic estimates and their uncertainty.
Moderately important I feel that if there is non-independence it would be reflected in the chosen statistical model. If the authors are not aware of non-independence, then, ultimately, the chosen statistical model would likely not be optimal for the data set anyway.
Extremely important There is no such thing as non-independence. That is the central problem of meta-analysis. There is always a confounding influence. We see a flood of meta-analysis (recently mostly from researchers in China), that irons the data flat. Whatever response meta-analysis aims at distilling depends on the quality of the handling of confounding variables. This is not normally something that statistics experts can do. In the end we often see meta-analysis the outcome of which reflects the frequency distribution of methods. For instance, if 95% of the data come from potted plants and 5% from trees in nature, the outcome will be dominated by what potted plants do, no matter how sophisticated the meta-analysis is.
Extremely important To avoid biased results, it is important to report a non-independent effect size estimated.
Very important Yes! And very often underreported (or not even considered)
Extremely important For checking assumptions and validate the statistical methods used.
Extremely important I think this is the least understood aspect of MA (especially for researchers new to MA) and so it is often not reported. But not appropriately handling non-independence will lead to incorrect conclusions so authors need to report this.
